list.listitem: All patients with suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), including those with mild symptoms after an otherwise typical thunderclap onset, should have an emergency CT scan without contrast interpreted by an expert.A

Screen individuals with two or more affected first-degree relatives, identical twins if SAH has occurred in one of the pair, and patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease; begin at age 20 and screen approximately every 5 years.B

An RCT found that at 1 year in patients treated with coiling there was an absolute risk reduction of 7.4% (NNT = 14) for the combined outcome death or dependency in comparison to patients treated with clipping.A
Around one-third of survivors of SAH are dependent, often with cognitive impairment, and two-thirds have a reduced quality of life.B

background.definition: Nontraumatic SAH is a neurological emergency characterized by the extravasation of blood into the spaces covering the central nervous system that are filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

list.listitem: Worldwide: 10.5 (95% CI, 9.9-11.2) cases per 100,000 people per year.
Finland: 22.0 (95% CI, 20.0-23.0) cases per 100,000 people per year.
Japan: 23.0 (95% CI, 19.0-28.0) per 100,000 people per year.
Other regions: 7.8 (95% CI, 7.2-8.4) per 100,000 people per year.
Women: 7.1 (95% CI, 5.4-8.7) per 100,000 people per year.
Men: 4.5 (95% CI, 3.1-5.8) per 100,000 people per year.
The incidence increases with age, with a mean age at presentation of 55 years.
SAH accounts for 2% to 5% of all new strokes, with an estimated frequency of 21,000 to 33,000 people each year in the United States.
Ruptured cerebral aneurysm is the most common cause of SAH (85%).
Non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic hemorrhage is responsible for approximately 10% of SAH.

Other rare conditions make up approximately 5% of SAH and are listed below: Inflammatory lesions of cerebral arteries: mycotic aneurysm, borreliosis, Behcet's disease, primary angiitis, polyarteritis nodosa, Churg-Strauss syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis. Non vascular lesions of intracerebral vessels: arterial dissection, cerebral arteriovenous malformations, fusiform aneurysm, cerebral dural arteriovenous fistulae, intracerebral cavernous angioma, cerebral venous thrombosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, Moyamoya disease. Vascular lesions of the spinal cord: saccular aneurysm of spinal artery, spinal arteriovenous fistula or malformation, cavernous angioma at spinal level. Tumors: pituitary apoplexy, cerebral metastases of cardiac myxoma, malignant glioma, acoustic neuroma, angiolipoma, Schwannoma of cranial nerve, cervical meningiomas, cervical spinal cord hemangioblastoma, spinal meningeal carcinomatosis, melanoma of the cauda equine. Drugs: cocaine abuse, anticoagulants. Other: sickle cell disease, coagulopathies, and patients without identifiable cause.
The main cause of SAH is the rupture of an intracranial aneurysm. Intracranial aneurisms are not congenital, as was once believed, but develop in the course of life.
SAH occurs when the site of hemorrhage is in the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain.

Screen individuals for aneurysm with two or more affected first-degree relatives, identical twins if SAH has occurred in one of the pair, and patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (13% prevalence); begin at age 20 and screen approximately every 5 years.BThe yield of long term screening has been supported by longitudinal studies.
Among persons with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, risk is higher in women, those with a family histor of SAH or aneurysm, and those with moderate or severe chronic kidney disease.
Female smokers age 50 to 60 years had a 10% rate of undetected intracranial aneurysm in a Finnish series of 108 women. Most (8/11) were < 5 mm.

Individuals with a single affected first-degree relative have a 5 to 12 times greater lifetime risk of SAH than the general population. However, the chance of findings an aneurysm by screening in an individual with a single affected relative is only 1.7 times higher than in the general population. In individuals with only a single affected first-degree relative, screening is not efficient or effective (NNT = 300).B

Although patients who have survived a sporadic episode of SAH are at increased risk of a new episode from a new aneurysm or from recurrence of the treated aneurysm, screening of these patients is generally not recommended except in those (especially women) with an initial episode at very young age and multiple aneurysms at time of the initial SAH.C
Statin use was associated with a lower risk of SAH in a case-control study with 3498 cases and 13,992 matched controls (aOR 0.81).
All patients with suspected SAH, including those with mild symptoms after an otherwise typical thunderclap onset, should have an emergency CT scan without contrast interpreted by an expert.A
If CT scanning is considered normal (uncommon in the first 24 hours after aneurysm rupture), lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis must be performed.A

Digital subtraction cerebral angiography has been the gold standard for the detection of cerebral aneurysm, but CT angiography has gained popularity and is frequently used owing to its noninvasiveness and a sensitivity and specificity comparable to that of cerebral angiography.B

list.listitem: Sudden death occurs in 10% of patients with spontaneous SAH.

Patients typically present with sudden severe headache that is maximal in intensity immediately or within minutes and lasts an hour or more (up to days). Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and neck stiffness. Loss of consciousness, either transient at onset (around 50% of cases) or persisting, is common. Seizures occur in 1 of every 14 patients.
A systematic review found that the typical symptoms and signs of SAH had low accuracy for the diagnosis, with neck pain and stiffness and the most helpful clinical findings.
Focal neurological symptoms such as dysphasia, hemisensory, or motor symptoms may occur at the same time as the headache or soon afterward in one-third of patients.
Complication of aneurysmal SAH include rebleeding, immediate or delayed cerebral ischemia, hydrocephalus, and seizures.
Misdiagnosis in the emergency department can occur in up to 9% of patients presenting with acute cerebrovascular illness, and more likely in the setting of mild, non-specific, or transient symptoms.

Emergent brain CT scan without contrast is the first investigation if SAH is suspected. CT scan is normal in most patients with sudden headache, but to exclude SAH, a carefully planned lumbar puncture is also needed. Even with a normal neurologic exam, headache syndromes concerning for SAH should be evaluated first with a brain CT scan prior to proceeding with lumbar puncture.

Patients with SAH proved by imaging or lumbar puncture should have invasive arteriography. This serves not only to identify one or more aneurysms as potential causes in a patient with SAH but also to study the anatomical configuration of the aneurysm in relation to adjoining arteries, which allows optimum selection of treatment (coiling or clipping).
MR angiography and CT angiography are accurate for patients with suspected aneurysm; transcranial Doppler ultrasound is less accurate.
A validated clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of major bleeding complications, including SAH, in patients taking warfarin.

The Ottawa Headache score predicts the likelihood of subarachnoid hemorrhage in persons with acute headache. Imaging is recommended if any of the following are present: symptom of neck pain or stiffness, age > 40 years, witnessed loss of consciousness, onset during exertion, thunderclap headache (peak pain instantly), or limited neck flexion upon exam. The rule is 99% sensitive but only 27% specific.

The A4C risk score is more accurate than others at predicting bleeding risk in elderly patients taking a DOAC. It has 5 items: increasingn age, decreasing eGFR, hemoglobin < 11 g/dl, albumin < 35 g/L and amiodarone use.
Suspect SAH in patients presenting with sudden headache.
The best initial imaging study is brain CT scan without contrast.
If the initial study is negative but suspicion for SAH persists, lumbar puncture should be performed.
If the examination is positive, brain MRI or conventional angiography should be performed and a neurosurgeon urgently consulted.

The International Aneurysm Trial (ISAT) clinical trial found that at 1 year in patients treated with coiling there was an absolute risk reduction of 7.4% (NNT = 14) for the combined outcome death or dependency in comparison to patients treated with clipping.A
Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 3 weeks reduces risk of poor outcome and delayed cerebral ischemia (NNT = 20).B

Fluid management has been used to prevent hypovolemia and sodium depletion (with administration of 3 liters IV 0.9% saline daily), since a reduction in plasma volume may contribute to the development of cerebral ischemia. However, a recent Cochrane review concluded from several small studies that there is no sound evidence for the use of volume expansion in patients with a SAH from an aneurysm.
IV fluid therapy with colloids or blood transfusions have been associated with an increased rates of unfavorable outcomes at discharge and at 6 months.

A trial randomized 742 adults with acute aneurysmal SAH and anemia to a liberal strategy ( mandatory transfusion at hemoglobin <= 10 g/dl or a restrictive strategy (optional transfusion at <= 8 g/dl). A more liberal strategy did not reduce the risk of unfavorable one year outcomes.

A study randomized 108 patients with aneurysmal SAH to usual care or goal directed hemodynamic therapy. The likelihood of delayed cerebral ischemia was lower in the goal-directed group (13% vs 32%, p = 0.02) and a better functional outcome at 3 months. The goal directed therapy included advanced hemodynamic monitoring including transpulmonary thermodilution was performed to direct the volume therapy and followed an algorithm to guide use of fluids, norepinephrine, and dobutamine.
A recent Cochrane review concluded that antifibrinolytic therapy (tranexamic acid, epsioln amino-caproic acid, or equivalent) did not reduce the risk of death, vegetative state, or severe disability.
The lack of benefit of early tranexamic acid after subarachnoic hemorrhage was confirmed in a well designed and adequately powered randomized trial with 955 Dutch patients.

To prevent secondary central ischemia, oral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for 3 weeks) reduces risk (absolute 5%, relative 18%) of poor outcome and delayed cerebral ischemia. The NNT to prevent death or dependency is 19 if nimodipine is given within 10 days of hemorrhage.
A systematic review of four good quality studies comparing antiplatelet agents with placebo found a trend toward better outcomes in patients with aneurysmal SAH.
While tirilazad has neuroprotective effects in animal studies, there is no clinical benefit of adding tirilazad to nimodipine therapy in human subjects with SAH.

Restarting anticoagulant therapy in patients with intracranial hemorrage was associated in one study with reduced thromboembolic events with similar rates (8%-9%) of recurrent hemorrhage compared to patients taken off anticoagulation.
A randomized trial with 409 patients with surgically treated aneurysmal SAH compared clazosentan with placebo but found no benefit.

To prevent rebleeding, aneurysm ablation should be performed: aneurysm ablation timed as early as possible to maximally prevent aneurysm rebleeding is a uniform policy in most centers. ISAT found that at 1 year there was no difference in fatality rate between aneurysm clipping and endovascular coiling, but for combined death and dependent rates there was an absolute risk reduction of 7.4% (NNT = 14) associated with coiling, which is statistically significant.
There is limited evidence to support the timing of aneurysm surgery after SAH. Most surgeons currently operate within 3 to 4 days of presentation to prevent rebleeding.
To treat hydrocephalus, external drainage of the cerebrospinal fluid by a catheter inserted through a burr hole should be performed.
To treat delayed cerebral ischemia, some centers have experience with the endovascular approach (transluminal angioplasty or direct vasodilators) in the treatment of symptomatic vasospasm after SAH.
A recent meta-analysis found that early decompressive craniectomy for intracranial hemorrhage does not seem to significantly reduce mortality when compared to medical therapy.

In patients with intracranial aneurysms previously treated by endovascular coiling, microsurgical treatment of residual or recurrent aneurysms was generally successful. In a series of 883 procedures, complete occlusion was achieved in 97.2% and improved or unchanged functional outcomes in 92.3%.
Patients with ruptured aneurysm should be immediately transferred to an institution with a comprehensive neurosurgical service.
Rebleeding (without aneurysm occlusion) occurs in 15% on day 1, 40% by 1 month, and after 6 months at a rate of 3% per year.

To prevent rebleeding, aneurysm ablation timed as early as possible should be performed and antifibrinolytic drugs could be used (tranexamic acid 1 g IV followed by 1 g every 6 hours until aneurysm repair is carried out as soon as possible).

Immediate cerebral ischemia may occur from raised intracranial pressure and hence reduced cerebral perfusion pressure. To prevent secondary cerebral ischemia, oral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for 3 weeks) should be used with fluid management (3 liters IV 0.9% saline daily).
Delayed cerebral ischemia peaks between days 4 and 14 after SAH. To treat delayed cerebral ischemia, hypervolemia, hemodilution, and induced hypertension may be helpful.

To treat hydrocephalus, external drainage of the cerebrospinal fluid by a catheter inserted through a burr hole should be performed. The benefit of this approach in affecting overall mortality is under investigation.

Monitoring and management of patients with an SAH should take place in an intensive care setting because of the acuity of the condition, frequent elevations in intracranial pressure and blood pressure, frequent need for intubation and assisted ventilation, and multiple complicating medical issues.

This post-hoc analysis showed that intensive SBP reduction for patients who present with intracerebral hemorrhage and excessively high SBP (>220 mm Hg) results in a higher rate of neurological deterioration in 24 hours. Despite this, the rate of hematoma expansion within 24 hours and the risk of death or severe disability at 90 days are not affected.

In patients without a history of SAH, untreated aneurysms <10 mm in diameter have an annual rupture rate of 0.05%. The risks of rupture in those 10 to 25 mm (1% per year) and >25 mm (6% per year) are much higher. The risks of surgery-related death and disability are 3.8% and 12% at 1 year. Aneurysms in the basilar tip, or in the vertebrobasilar or posterior cerebral circulation, are more likely to rupture (RR = 13.6).

A contemporary series identified 661 patients with 767 unruptured intracranial aneurysms who were managed conservatively. The annual rupture rate was 0.6%, with 87% occurring within 5 years and none after 10 years of follow-up.
In population-based studies the overall case fatality rate was about 50%.B
In the community, case fatality is 12%, and a further 10% of those who reach hospital alive die within 24 hours.B
Around one-third of survivors of SAH are dependent, often with cognitive impairment, and two-thirds have a reduced quality of life.B

In a series of 1564 patients at a single center with SAH, 21% had a poor functional outcome at one year. Predictors of a poor outcome include increasing age, troponin, and S100-beta levels; surgical or coiling complications, hydrocephalus requiring drainage, and incomplete aneurysm occlusion.
